title: Why Your AI Agents Keep Failing (And How One Diagram Fixes It)

shots.scriptText: Every AI agent tutorial you have watched is lying to you. They show you one agent, doing one task, in a straight line. Prompt in, answer out. Looks great in a demo.

blocks.title: Linear Pipeline
blocks.body: Single prompt in, single answer out. Fails immediately in production.

shots.scriptText: Then you try to build something real - five agents, one goal - and it falls apart. Agents talk over each other. State gets lost. One agent loops forever and burns your API budget while you are asleep.

blocks.caption: TEA-1 Physical Embodiment · Multi-Joint Contact Dynamics

shots.scriptText: There is a reason for that. And there is a fix. It is called graph engineering - and once you see it, you cannot unsee it.

Here is the mental shift. A single AI agent is not one call to a model. It is a loop. Think. Act. Look at the result. Think again. You cannot draw a loop with an arrow that only points forward. A straight line cannot come back on itself.

blocks.caption: Step 1: Think → Step 2: Act → Step 3: Observe → Step 4: Loop

blocks.title: The 4-Step Cycle
blocks.body: A single agent is not a forward line. It is a continuous re-evaluation loop.

shots.scriptText: So the moment you need looping - or branching, or five agents working at once - a straight chain breaks. You need a graph. Nodes. Edges. And something flowing between them.

Every graph-based agent system runs on four things. One - state. A shared object every agent reads and writes to. Not 'the conversation.' Real structured data: the task, the plan, the results so far, and the errors.

blocks.title: Typed State Object
blocks.body: Stores task spec, plan checkpoints, error registers, and partial payloads.

shots.scriptText: Two - nodes. Each one does one job: an LLM call, a tool call, or a human checkpoint. Nodes can contain entire agents inside them - nesting like Russian dolls. Three - edges. Conditional edges: a function that looks at the state and asks, 'what happens next?'

blocks.note: Dynamic routing functions evaluate current state

shots.scriptText: This - right here - is the actual engineering. Not the prompts. The routing. And four - checkpoints. Save state after every step. When an agent runs for ten minutes and step forty-one crashes, you do not want to lose steps one through forty.

blocks.title: Crash Recovery
blocks.body: Persisting state per step allows instant rewind and resumed execution.

shots.scriptText: Okay. Here is how you actually go from one agent to an army. Pattern one: the Supervisor. Picture a general and five soldiers. The soldiers never talk to each other - they report back to the general, who decides who moves next. One brain, many hands.

blocks.caption: TEA-1 Physical Embodiment · Multi-Joint Contact Dynamics

blocks.text: SUPERVISOR PATTERN · ONE BRAIN MANY HANDS

shots.scriptText: Pattern two: Fan-out, fan-in. This is the real army move. Say you need to research five competitors. You do not send one agent to do it five times in a row - you spawn five agents at once, each takes one competitor, and they all report back to a single reducer that merges the results.

blocks.note: 5x throughput speedup via parallel agent dispatch

blocks.title: Map-Reduce Reducer
blocks.body: Dispatches N worker agents and aggregates into a single merged record.

shots.scriptText: But here is the trap almost everyone falls into: if two agents write to the same piece of state at the same time, and you have not told your system how to merge them - one silently erases the other's work. Nobody warns you about this. I am warning you.

Pattern three: Hierarchical. Once you are past five or six agents, one supervisor gets overwhelmed. So supervisors get their own sub-supervisors. Teams of teams. That is how you actually scale this past a demo.

blocks.title: Sub-Supervisors
blocks.body: Nested supervisory trees scale cleanly to dozens of autonomous agents.

shots.scriptText: Three things will bite you the first time you build this for real. Loops that never end - because you asked an AI 'are we done yet?' and it cannot decide. Fix: always cap it with a hard iteration limit.

Cost that quietly explodes - because every hop through your graph is a full model call. And debugging - in a graph, you must log every state change at every step, or you will be flying blind. These are not edge cases. These are Tuesday.

blocks.note: Granular state tracing prevents compounding error costs

blocks.title: State Telemetry
blocks.body: Record inputs, outputs, and diffs on every step for deterministic debugging.

shots.scriptText: So here is the whole idea in one image: Stop thinking about your agents as a line. Start thinking about them as a map - with a shared memory, decision points at every fork, and a plan for what happens when five paths need to become one.

The agents you have been building? They were never the hard part. The coordination between them - that is the actual skill. That is the part nobody teaches. And now you know it. If this made something click for you - go build your army.

blocks.title: Master The Coordination
blocks.body: The prompt is just the worker. The graph is the organization.
